paper.title: Expected PGT paper 3 · harder level
paper.source: Written by GS HOUSE for the UP PGT Mathematics exam expected in December 2026, in the pattern of the UP PGT paper of 10 May 2026 and the official syllabus: 30 questions asked in earlier papers (19 from UPPSC GIC 2015 and 11 from UP PGT 2013; each solved again, misprints repaired) and 60 new; every question checked by a second mathematician

src.label: Expected PGT 3 · Q1 · asked in UPPSC GIC 2015

en.q: The co-ordinates of the vector $(2,1,-6)$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ relative to the basis $\{(1,1,2),\ (3,-1,0),\ (2,0,-1)\}$ of $\mathbb{R}^3(\mathbb{R})$ are given by
en.explanation: Solve $\alpha(1,1,2)+\beta(3,-1,0)+\gamma(2,0,-1)=(2,1,-6)$: $\alpha-\beta=1$, $2\alpha-\gamma=-6$, $\alpha+3\beta+2\gamma=2$. With $\alpha=1+\beta$, $\gamma=8+2\beta$: $1+\beta+3\beta+16+4\beta=2$, so $\beta=-\frac{15}8$, $\alpha=-\frac78$, $\gamma=\frac{17}4$.
facts: Co-ordinates relative to a basis = the unique coefficients of the linear combination.

en.q: Which of the following subsets of the vector space $M_2(\mathbb{R})$ of all $2\times2$ real matrices is a subspace?
options: The set of all symmetric matrices
The set of all invertible matrices
The set of all matrices with determinant 0
The set of all matrices with trace 1
en.explanation: Symmetric matrices: $O^T=O$, and if $A^T=A$, $B^T=B$ then $(\alpha A+\beta B)^T=\alpha A+\beta B$; so they form a subspace. The others fail: $O$ is not invertible; $\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}=I$ has determinant 1; the zero matrix has trace 0.
notes: Correct: contains $O$ and is closed under $\alpha A+\beta B$.
Does not contain the zero matrix.
Does not contain the zero matrix (trace 0).
facts: Subspace test: contains the zero vector and is closed under $\alpha u+\beta v$; a set cut out by linear homogeneous conditions passes it.

en.q: The number of arrangements of the letters of the word ARRANGE in which the two R's do not come together is
en.explanation: ARRANGE has 7 letters with A twice and R twice: total $\frac{7!}{2!\,2!}=1260$. With the R's tied together: $\frac{6!}{2!}=360$. Required $1260-360=900$.
notes: Arrangements with the two R's together.
facts: 'Not together' = total − 'together'.

src.label: Expected PGT 3 · Q4 · asked in UPPSC GIC 2015

en.q: If $y^a$ is an integrating factor of the differential equation $2xy\,dx-(3x^2-y^2)\,dy=0$, then the value of $a$ is
en.explanation: Multiply by $y^a$: $M=2xy^{a+1}$, $N=-3x^2y^a+y^{a+2}$. Exactness needs $\frac{\partial M}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial N}{\partial x}$: $2(a+1)xy^a=-6xy^a$, so $a+1=-3$, $a=-4$.
facts: An integrating factor makes $M_y=N_x$; for $y^a$ compare the coefficients of $xy^a$.

en.q: The number of ordered triples $(x,y,z)$ of positive integers such that $xyz=24$ is
en.explanation: $24=2^3\cdot3$. Distribute the three 2's among $x,y,z$: $\binom{3+2}{2}=10$ ways; the single 3: 3 ways. Total $10\times3=30$.
facts: Ordered factorisations of $p^a$ into $k$ factors: $\binom{a+k-1}{k-1}$; multiply over the primes.

en.q: Match List – I (Differential equation, $D\equiv\frac{d}{dx}$) with List – II (General solution). List – I: a. $(D^2+4)y=0$, b. $(D^2-4)y=0$, c. $(D-2)^2y=0$, d. $(D^2+4D+5)y=0$. List – II: I. $y=(c_1+c_2x)e^{2x}$, II. $y=c_1e^{2x}+c_2e^{-2x}$, III. $y=e^{-2x}(c_1\cos x+c_2\sin x)$, IV. $y=c_1\cos2x+c_2\sin2x$. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: a – IV, b – I, c – II, d – III
a – IV, b – II, c – III, d – I
a – II, b – IV, c – I, d – III
a – IV, b – II, c – I, d – III
en.explanation: Auxiliary equations: a. $m=\pm2i$ → $c_1\cos2x+c_2\sin2x$. b. $m=\pm2$ → $c_1e^{2x}+c_2e^{-2x}$. c. $m=2,2$ → $(c_1+c_2x)e^{2x}$. d. $m=-2\pm i$ → $e^{-2x}(c_1\cos x+c_2\sin x)$.
notes: Confuses a repeated root with distinct roots.
facts: Roots $\alpha\pm i\beta$ give $e^{\alpha x}(c_1\cos\beta x+c_2\sin\beta x)$; a repeated root $m$ gives $(c_1+c_2x)e^{mx}$.

en.q: In a triangle $ABC$, if $r_1=2r_2=3r_3$, then $a:b:c$ is
en.explanation: $r_1=\frac\Delta{s-a}$ etc., so $\frac1{s-a}:\frac1{s-b}:\frac1{s-c}=6:3:2$ and $(s-a):(s-b):(s-c)=1:2:3$. Put $s-a=k$, $s-b=2k$, $s-c=3k$; adding, $s=6k$, so $a=5k$, $b=4k$, $c=3k$.
facts: Ex-radii: $r_1=\frac{\Delta}{s-a}$, $r_2=\frac{\Delta}{s-b}$, $r_3=\frac{\Delta}{s-c}$.

en.q: If $x,y,z$ are positive real numbers, none equal to 1, then the value of $\begin{vmatrix}1&\log_xy&\log_xz\\\log_yx&1&\log_yz\\\log_zx&\log_zy&1\end{vmatrix}$ is
en.explanation: Write $\log_ab=\frac{\log b}{\log a}$. Multiplying $R_1,R_2,R_3$ by $\log x,\log y,\log z$ turns every row into $(\log x,\ \log y,\ \log z)$. So the rows are proportional and the determinant is 0.
notes: Takes only the product of the diagonal entries.
$\log x+\log y+\log z$ is the sum of the common row $(\log x,\log y,\log z)$, not the determinant; equal rows give 0.
Sign slip on the diagonal product 1; a determinant with proportional rows is 0.
facts: A determinant with proportional rows (or columns) is 0; $\log_ab=\frac{\log b}{\log a}$.

en.q: The moment of inertia of a uniform solid right circular cone of mass $M$ and base radius $a$ about its axis is
en.explanation: Slice the cone (height $h$) into discs. The disc at distance $x$ from the vertex has radius $\frac{ax}h$ and mass $\frac{3M}{h^3}x^2dx$ (since $M=\rho\cdot\frac13\pi a^2h$); its moment about the axis is $\frac12\cdot\frac{3M}{h^3}x^2dx\cdot\frac{a^2x^2}{h^2}$. So $I=\frac{3Ma^2}{2h^5}\int_0^hx^4dx=\frac{3Ma^2}{10}$.
notes: That is a solid cylinder (or disc) about its axis.
That is a solid sphere about a diameter.
Uses $mr^2$ instead of $\frac12mr^2$ for each disc, which doubles the true value.
facts: Solid cone about its axis $\frac3{10}Ma^2$: less than a cylinder's $\frac12Ma^2$, because more of the mass lies near the axis.

en.q: The value of $\sum_{k=1}^{6}\left(\sin\frac{2\pi k}{7}-i\cos\frac{2\pi k}{7}\right)$ is
en.explanation: $\sin\theta-i\cos\theta=-i(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)$. The numbers $e^{2\pi ik/7}$, $k=1,\dots,6$, are the non-real 7th roots of unity and add to $-1$. So the sum is $-i(-1)=i$.
notes: Forgets that the root 1 is missing from the sum.
path: 10.4 Polar form, Euler's form and De Moivre's theorem
facts: The $n$th roots of unity add to 0, so those other than 1 add to $-1$.

en.q: Which of the following statements are correct? a. The eigenvalues of a real symmetric matrix are real. b. Every eigenvalue of a real orthogonal matrix is 1 or $-1$. c. A square matrix and its transpose have the same eigenvalues. d. If $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$, then $\lambda^2$ is an eigenvalue of $A^2$. Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
en.explanation: a: true (spectral theorem). b: false — the eigenvalues of an orthogonal matrix have modulus 1; the rotation $\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $\pm i$. c: true, since $\det(A^T-\lambda I)=\det(A-\lambda I)$. d: true, $A^2x=\lambda Ax=\lambda^2x$.
facts: Orthogonal: $|\lambda|=1$; symmetric: $\lambda$ real; skew-symmetric: $\lambda$ zero or purely imaginary.

en.q: $\int\frac{dx}{\sin x+\cos x}$ is equal to ($C$ is an arbitrary constant)
en.explanation: $\sin x+\cos x=\sqrt2\sin\left(x+\frac\pi4\right)$. So the integral is $\frac1{\sqrt2}\int\operatorname{cosec}\left(x+\frac\pi4\right)dx=\frac1{\sqrt2}\log\left|\tan\left(\frac x2+\frac\pi8\right)\right|+C$.
notes: That is $\frac1{\sqrt2}\int\sec\left(x+\frac\pi4\right)dx$; the sum is $\sqrt2\sin\left(x+\frac\pi4\right)$, not $\sqrt2\cos$.
facts: $\int\operatorname{cosec}u\,du=\log\left|\tan\frac u2\right|$; $a\sin x+b\cos x=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\sin(x+\alpha)$.

en.q: Let $V$ be the vector space of real polynomials of degree at most 3. The dimension of the subspace $W=\{p\in V: p(1)=0,\ p'(1)=0\}$ is
en.explanation: $p(1)=p'(1)=0$ means $(x-1)^2$ divides $p$, so $p=(x-1)^2(ax+b)$. The two free constants give $\dim W=2$ (basis $(x-1)^2$, $x(x-1)^2$). Equivalently $4-2=2$ independent conditions.
notes: Uses only one of the two conditions.
facts: Each independent linear condition lowers the dimension by 1.

src.label: Expected PGT 3 · Q14 · asked in UPPSC GIC 2015

en.q: Given $f'(2)=6$ and $f'(1)=4$, then $\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(2h+2+h^2)-f(2)}{f(h-h^2+1)-f(1)}$ is equal to
en.explanation: The limit is of the form $\frac00$. By L'Hospital's rule it equals $\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f'(2h+2+h^2)(2+2h)}{f'(h-h^2+1)(1-2h)}=\frac{f'(2)\cdot2}{f'(1)\cdot1}=\frac{12}{4}=3$.
notes: Forgets the factor 2 from the inner derivative $2+2h$.
facts: L'Hospital with the chain rule: $\frac{d}{dh}f(g(h))=f'(g(h))g'(h)$.

src.label: Expected PGT 3 · Q15 · asked in UPPSC GIC 2015

en.q: The angle between the pair of planes $2x^2-6y^2-12z^2+18yz+2zx+xy=0$ is
en.explanation: The equation factorises as $(2x-3y+6z)(x+2y-2z)=0$. The normals $(2,-3,6)$ and $(1,2,-2)$ have lengths 7 and 3 and dot product $2-6-12=-16$, so $\cos\theta=\frac{16}{21}$. (Formula check: $\tan\theta=\frac{2\sqrt{f^2+g^2+h^2-bc-ca-ab}}{a+b+c}$ gives $\frac{\sqrt{185}}{16}$ in size.)
facts: Angle between the planes of $ax^2+by^2+cz^2+2fyz+2gzx+2hxy=0$: $\tan\theta=\frac{2\sqrt{f^2+g^2+h^2-bc-ca-ab}}{a+b+c}$.

en.q: Match List – I (Uniform body; point of reference) with List – II (Distance of its centre of gravity from that point). List – I: a. hollow right circular cone (curved surface only) of height $h$; from the centre of its base, b. solid paraboloid of revolution of height $h$; from its vertex, c. circular sector of radius $a$ and angle $2\alpha$; from the centre, d. quadrant of a circular disc of radius $a$; from the centre. List – II: I. $\frac{2h}3$, II. $\frac{4\sqrt2\,a}{3\pi}$, III. $\frac h3$, IV. $\frac{2a\sin\alpha}{3\alpha}$. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: a – I, b – III, c – IV, d – II
a – III, b – I, c – IV, d – II
a – III, b – I, c – II, d – IV
a – IV, b – I, c – III, d – II
en.explanation: a. The ring of the curved surface at distance $x$ from the vertex has area $\propto x\,dx$, so $\bar x=\frac{\int_0^hx^2dx}{\int_0^hx\,dx}=\frac{2h}3$ from the vertex, i.e. $\frac h3$ from the base. b. For $y^2=4kx$, $0\le x\le h$: $\bar x=\frac{\int_0^hx\,y^2dx}{\int_0^hy^2dx}=\frac{h^3/3}{h^2/2}=\frac{2h}3$. c. Sector: $\frac{2a\sin\alpha}{3\alpha}$ (two-thirds of the arc's $\frac{a\sin\alpha}\alpha$). d. The quadrant's centre of gravity is $\left(\frac{4a}{3\pi},\frac{4a}{3\pi}\right)$, at distance $\frac{4\sqrt2\,a}{3\pi}$ from the centre.
facts: Hollow cone $\frac h3$ and solid cone $\frac h4$ from the base; solid paraboloid $\frac{2h}3$ from the vertex; sector $\frac{2a\sin\alpha}{3\alpha}$, arc $\frac{a\sin\alpha}{\alpha}$ from the centre.

en.q: The number of subgroups of order 12 in a cyclic group of order 60 is
en.explanation: A cyclic group of order $n$ has exactly one subgroup of each order $d$ dividing $n$: if $G=\langle a\rangle$ it is $\langle a^{n/d}\rangle$. Since $12\mid60$, there is exactly one, $\langle a^5\rangle$.
notes: $\varphi(12)=4$ counts the generators of that subgroup (the elements of order 12), not subgroups.
Correct: exactly one subgroup for each divisor of 60.
12 divides 60, so such a subgroup exists.
$\frac{60}{12}=5$ is the index of the subgroup.
facts: Every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic, and for each $d\mid n$ a cyclic group of order $n$ has exactly one subgroup of order $d$.

src.label: Expected PGT 3 · Q18 · asked in UPPSC GIC 2015

en.q: The tangents from which of the following points to the ellipse $4x^2+5y^2=20$ are perpendicular?
en.explanation: The ellipse is $\frac{x^2}{5}+\frac{y^2}{4}=1$. Perpendicular tangents meet on the director circle $x^2+y^2=a^2+b^2=9$. Only $(1,2\sqrt2)$ satisfies it: $1+8=9$.
facts: Director circle of $\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$: $x^2+y^2=a^2+b^2$.

en.q: The general solution of $\sin x+\sin2x+\sin3x=0$ is ($n\in\mathbb{Z}$)
en.explanation: $\sin x+\sin3x=2\sin2x\cos x$, so the equation is $\sin2x\,(2\cos x+1)=0$. Either $\sin2x=0$, i.e. $x=\frac{n\pi}2$, or $\cos x=-\frac12$, i.e. $x=2n\pi\pm\frac{2\pi}3$. Both families are needed.
facts: Pair terms by sum-to-product ($\sin A+\sin B=2\sin\frac{A+B}2\cos\frac{A-B}2$), factorise, and keep every factor.

en.q: Two unlike parallel forces of 10 N and 6 N act at the points $A$ and $B$ of a rod, where $AB=20$ cm. The line of action of their resultant meets the line $AB$ at a point $C$ outside the segment $AB$. The length $AC$ is
en.explanation: The resultant is $10-6=4$ N, parallel to the larger force, and acts at $C$ on $BA$ produced beyond $A$ with $10\cdot CA=6\cdot CB$. Putting $CB=CA+20$: $10\,CA=6\,CA+120$, so $CA=30$ cm (and $CB=50$ cm).
notes: That is $CB$, the distance from the smaller force.
Uses $10\cdot AC=6\cdot AB$, forgetting that $C$ lies outside $AB$.
path: 15.3 Coplanar forces, moments and parallel forces
facts: Unlike parallel forces $P>Q$: resultant $P-Q$, acting outside $AB$ on the side of $P$, with $P\cdot CA=Q\cdot CB$.

en.q: Which of the following binary operations on $\mathbb{Z}$ is both commutative and associative?
en.explanation: $a+b+ab$ is symmetric in $a,b$, and $(a*b)*c=a+b+c+ab+bc+ca+abc=a*(b*c)$. The others fail: $1-2\ne2-1$; $2\cdot1+2=4\ne2\cdot2+1=5$; $(1*2)*3=|1-3|=2$ but $1*(2*3)=|1-1|=0$.
facts: $a*b=a+b+ab$ is multiplication in disguise: $1+(a*b)=(1+a)(1+b)$.

en.q: If $\vec a\ne\vec0$ and $\vec a\times\vec b=\vec a\times\vec c$, then which of the following is necessarily true?
options: $\vec b-\vec c$ is parallel to $\vec a$
$\vec b-\vec c$ is perpendicular to $\vec a$
en.explanation: $\vec a\times(\vec b-\vec c)=\vec0$, so $\vec b-\vec c=\lambda\vec a$ for some scalar $\lambda$ (possibly 0): it is parallel to $\vec a$. Nothing forces $\lambda=0$: with $\vec a=\hat i$, $\vec b=\hat i+\hat j$, $\vec c=\hat j$ both products equal $\hat k$, yet $\vec b\ne\vec c$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec b=1\ne0=\vec a\cdot\vec c$.
notes: Cancels $\vec a$ as if a cross product could be divided.
That would follow from $\vec a\cdot\vec b=\vec a\cdot\vec c$, not from the cross products.
Fails for $\vec a=\hat i$, $\vec b=\hat i+\hat j$, $\vec c=\hat j$.
facts: $\vec a\times\vec u=\vec0$ with $\vec a\ne\vec0$ means $\vec u\parallel\vec a$; neither the dot nor the cross product can be cancelled.

src.label: Expected PGT 3 · Q23 · asked in UPPSC GIC 2015

en.q: If $S$ is the surface of the sphere $x^2+y^2+z^2=a^2$, then the value of $\iint_S\left(xy\,dy\,dz+y^2\,dz\,dx+yz\,dx\,dy\right)$ is equal to
en.explanation: This is the outward flux of $\vec F=xy\,\hat i+y^2\,\hat j+yz\,\hat k$ through $S$. By Gauss's divergence theorem it equals $\iiint_V\nabla\cdot\vec F\,dV=\iiint_V(y+2y+y)\,dV=4\iiint_Vy\,dV$. The ball is symmetric under $y\to-y$ and $y$ is odd, so the value is 0.
notes: Takes $\nabla\cdot\vec F=3$, as for $\vec r$: $3\times\frac43\pi a^3$.
That is the volume of the ball, as if $\nabla\cdot\vec F=1$.
path: 14.3 Line, surface and volume integrals; integral theorems
facts: Gauss: $\iint_S\vec F\cdot\hat n\,dS=\iiint_V\nabla\cdot\vec F\,dV$; an odd function of $y$ integrates to 0 over a region symmetric in $y$.

en.q: If $A=\begin{bmatrix}\cos\alpha&-\sin\alpha\\\sin\alpha&\cos\alpha\end{bmatrix}$, $0<\alpha<\pi$, and $A+A^T=I$, then $\alpha$ is
en.explanation: $A+A^T=\begin{bmatrix}2\cos\alpha&0\\0&2\cos\alpha\end{bmatrix}=I$ gives $\cos\alpha=\frac12$, so $\alpha=\frac\pi3$.
facts: The off-diagonal entries of a rotation matrix cancel in $A+A^T$.

en.q: If each of the pairs of lines $x^2-2pxy-y^2=0$ and $x^2-2qxy-y^2=0$ bisects the angles between the other pair, then
en.explanation: The bisectors of $ax^2+2hxy+by^2=0$ are $\frac{x^2-y^2}{a-b}=\frac{xy}h$. For $x^2-2pxy-y^2=0$ ($a=1,b=-1,h=-p$): $\frac{x^2-y^2}{2}=-\frac{xy}p$, i.e. $x^2+\frac2pxy-y^2=0$. This is $x^2-2qxy-y^2=0$ iff $-2q=\frac2p$, i.e. $pq=-1$.
notes: Then the two pairs would coincide.
facts: Bisectors of $ax^2+2hxy+by^2=0$: $\frac{x^2-y^2}{a-b}=\frac{xy}{h}$.

src.label: Expected PGT 3 · Q26 · asked in UP PGT 2013

en.q: General solution of the differential equation $xp^2-yp+a=0$ $\left(p=\frac{dy}{dx}\right)$ is
en.explanation: Divide by $p$: $y=px+\frac ap$, which is Clairaut's equation $y=px+f(p)$. Its general solution is obtained by writing $c$ for $p$: $y=cx+\frac ac$, i.e. $xc^2-yc+a=0$.
notes: Correct: replace $p$ by $c$ in Clairaut's form.
facts: Clairaut's equation $y=px+f(p)$ has general solution $y=cx+f(c)$.

en.q: Which of the following sets is linearly independent in the vector space of all real-valued functions on $\mathbb{R}$?
en.explanation: If $a+bx+cx^2=0$ for all $x$, then $a=b=c=0$ (a non-zero polynomial has finitely many roots). Each other set has a non-trivial relation: $\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$; $2e^x=2\cdot e^x$; $\sin(x+1)=\cos1\sin x+\sin1\cos x$.
facts: Distinct powers $1,x,\dots,x^n$ are always linearly independent.

en.q: Match List – I (Solid generated by revolution about the $x$-axis) with List – II (Volume). List – I: a. the region under $y=\sqrt{a^2-x^2}$, $-a\le x\le a$, b. the region under $y=\frac rhx$, $0\le x\le h$, c. the region under $y=2\sqrt{ax}$, $0\le x\le h$, d. the region under $y=\sin x$, $0\le x\le\pi$. List – II: I. $2\pi ah^2$, II. $\frac{\pi^2}2$, III. $\frac43\pi a^3$, IV. $\frac13\pi r^2h$. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: a – III, b – IV, c – I, d – II
a – III, b – IV, c – II, d – I
a – I, b – IV, c – III, d – II
a – IV, b – III, c – I, d – II
en.explanation: $V=\pi\int y^2dx$. a: $\pi\int_{-a}^a(a^2-x^2)dx=\frac43\pi a^3$ (sphere). b: $\pi\int_0^h\frac{r^2x^2}{h^2}dx=\frac13\pi r^2h$ (cone). c: $\pi\int_0^h4ax\,dx=2\pi ah^2$ (paraboloid). d: $\pi\int_0^\pi\sin^2x\,dx=\frac{\pi^2}2$.
notes: Paraboloid and the sine solid swapped.
path: 7.6 Volumes and surfaces of solids of revolution — formulas
facts: Volume about the $x$-axis: $V=\pi\int_a^by^2\,dx$.

src.label: Expected PGT 3 · Q29 · asked in UP PGT 2013

en.q: If $1, Z_1, Z_2, \ldots, Z_{n-1}$ are the $n$th roots of unity, then $(1-Z_1)(1-Z_2)\cdots(1-Z_{n-1})$ is equal to
en.explanation: $x^n-1=(x-1)(x-Z_1)\cdots(x-Z_{n-1})$, so $(x-Z_1)\cdots(x-Z_{n-1})=1+x+\cdots+x^{n-1}$. Put $x=1$: the product is $n$.
notes: The factor $(1-1)$ is not in the product.
path: 10.4 Polar form, Euler's form and De Moivre's theorem

src.label: Expected PGT 3 · Q30 · asked in UPPSC GIC 2015

en.q: If $x+y=k$ is normal to the parabola $y^2=12x$, then the value of $k$ is
en.explanation: For $y^2=4ax$ ($a=3$) the normal of slope $m$ is $y=mx-2am-am^3$. With $m=-1$: $y=-x+6+3$, i.e. $x+y=9$. So $k=9$; it is the normal at $(3,6)$.
facts: Normal to $y^2=4ax$ in slope form: $y=mx-2am-am^3$.

en.q: $\int\frac{x^2+1}{x^4+1}dx$ is equal to ($C$ is an arbitrary constant)
en.explanation: Divide by $x^2$: $\int\frac{1+\frac1{x^2}}{x^2+\frac1{x^2}}dx$. Put $t=x-\frac1x$, $dt=\left(1+\frac1{x^2}\right)dx$, $x^2+\frac1{x^2}=t^2+2$. So the integral is $\frac1{\sqrt2}\tan^{-1}\frac t{\sqrt2}=\frac1{\sqrt2}\tan^{-1}\frac{x^2-1}{\sqrt2x}+C$.
facts: For $\frac{x^2\pm1}{x^4+1}$ divide by $x^2$ and put $t=x\mp\frac1x$.

src.label: Expected PGT 3 · Q32 · asked in UP PGT 2013

en.q: If $A=\begin{bmatrix}2&3\\5&-2\end{bmatrix}$, then $19A^{-1}$ is
en.explanation: $|A|=-4-15=-19$ and $\operatorname{adj}A=\begin{bmatrix}-2&-3\\-5&2\end{bmatrix}=-A$. So $A^{-1}=\frac{-A}{-19}=\frac{A}{19}$, i.e. $19A^{-1}=A$. (Equivalently $A^2=19I$.)
facts: For $A=\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&-a\end{bmatrix}$, $A^2=(a^2+bc)I$.

en.q: The differential equation of the family of circles touching the $x$-axis at the origin is
en.explanation: The circles are $x^2+y^2-2ky=0$ (centre $(0,k)$). Differentiating, $2x+2yy'-2ky'=0$, so $2k=\frac{2(x+yy')}{y'}$. Substituting: $(x^2+y^2)y'=2y(x+yy')$, i.e. $(x^2-y^2)\frac{dy}{dx}=2xy$.
notes: That is the family touching the $y$-axis at the origin.
facts: One arbitrary constant ⇒ differentiate once and eliminate it.

en.q: A straight line moves so that the sum of the reciprocals of its intercepts on the coordinate axes is $\frac14$. Then the line always passes through the point
en.explanation: The line is $\frac xa+\frac yb=1$ with $\frac1a+\frac1b=\frac14$. Then $\frac4a+\frac4b=1$, so $(4,4)$ lies on every such line.
notes: Takes the reciprocal the wrong way.
facts: A linear condition on $\frac1a,\frac1b$ makes $\frac xa+\frac yb=1$ pass through a fixed point.

en.q: The third term in the expansion of $x^4-3x^3$ in powers of $(x-2)$ is
en.explanation: By Taylor's theorem $f(x)=f(2)+f'(2)(x-2)+\frac{f''(2)}{2!}(x-2)^2+\cdots$. Here $f''(x)=12x^2-18x$, so $f''(2)=48-36=12$ and the third term is $\frac{12}{2}(x-2)^2=6(x-2)^2$. (The first two terms are $-8$ and $-4(x-2)$.)
facts: Coefficient of $(x-a)^k$ in a polynomial $=\frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k!}$.

en.q: If $\vec r=\vec a\cos\omega t+\vec b\sin\omega t$, where $\vec a,\vec b$ are constant vectors and $\omega$ is a constant, then $\vec r\times\frac{d\vec r}{dt}$ is equal to
en.explanation: $\frac{d\vec r}{dt}=-\omega\vec a\sin\omega t+\omega\vec b\cos\omega t$. Then $\vec r\times\frac{d\vec r}{dt}=\omega\cos^2\omega t\,(\vec a\times\vec b)-\omega\sin^2\omega t\,(\vec b\times\vec a)=\omega(\vec a\times\vec b)$.
notes: Order of the cross product reversed.
That is true of $\vec r\times\frac{d^2\vec r}{dt^2}$.
facts: $\vec b\times\vec a=-\vec a\times\vec b$ and $\vec a\times\vec a=\vec0$.

en.q: The centre of the conic $3x^2-2xy+3y^2+2x-6y+1=0$ is
en.explanation: The centre solves $\frac{\partial S}{\partial x}=6x-2y+2=0$ and $\frac{\partial S}{\partial y}=-2x+6y-6=0$. From the first $y=3x+1$; then $-2x+18x+6-6=0$ gives $x=0$, $y=1$.
path: 11.3 General equation of the second degree
facts: Centre of a central conic: solve $S_x=0$, $S_y=0$.

en.q: The locus of the mid-points of the chords of the circle $x^2+y^2=a^2$ which subtend a right angle at the centre is
en.explanation: A chord subtending $90^\circ$ at $O$ has its mid-point $M$ at distance $a\cos45^\circ=\frac{a}{\sqrt2}$ from $O$. So $M$ lies on $x^2+y^2=\frac{a^2}2$.
facts: Distance of a chord's mid-point from the centre $=r\cos\frac\theta2$ for a chord subtending $\theta$.

en.q: Which of the following statements are correct? a. Every group of prime order is cyclic. b. The order of every element of a finite group divides the order of the group. c. The alternating group $A_4$ has a subgroup of order 6. d. If $H$ is a subgroup of a finite group $G$, then the number of distinct left cosets of $H$ equals the number of distinct right cosets of $H$. Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
en.explanation: a: true — any $g\ne e$ has order dividing $p$, so it generates $G$. b: true (Lagrange applied to $\langle g\rangle$). c: false — $A_4$ (order 12) has no subgroup of order 6, so the converse of Lagrange fails. d: true — $aH\mapsto Ha^{-1}$ is a bijection; both numbers equal $[G:H]$.
notes: c is false and a is true.
facts: Lagrange: $o(H)\mid o(G)$; its converse is false ($A_4$ has no subgroup of order 6).

en.q: If $f(x)=\frac{\log\left(1+\frac xa\right)-\log\left(1-\frac xb\right)}{x}$ for $x\ne0$ is continuous at $x=0$, then $f(0)$ equals
en.explanation: $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\log(1+x/a)}{x}=\frac1a$ and $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\log(1-x/b)}{x}=-\frac1b$. So $f(0)=\frac1a-\left(-\frac1b\right)=\frac1a+\frac1b$.
notes: Sign slip in the second limit.
facts: $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\log(1+kx)}{x}=k$.

en.q: If $\cos x+\cos y=\frac13$ and $\sin x+\sin y=\frac14$, then $\tan\frac{x+y}2$ is
en.explanation: $\sin x+\sin y=2\sin\frac{x+y}2\cos\frac{x-y}2$ and $\cos x+\cos y=2\cos\frac{x+y}2\cos\frac{x-y}2$. Dividing, $\tan\frac{x+y}2=\frac{1/4}{1/3}=\frac34$.
facts: Sum-to-product: the common factor $2\cos\frac{x-y}2$ cancels.

en.q: If $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta$ are the roots of the equation $x^4+px^2+qx+k=0$, then the value of the product $(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)(\alpha+\gamma+\delta)(\alpha+\beta+\delta)(\beta+\gamma+\delta)$ is
en.explanation: There is no $x^3$ term, so $\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta=0$. Hence the four factors are $-\delta,-\beta,-\gamma,-\alpha$, and the product is $(-1)^4\alpha\beta\gamma\delta=\alpha\beta\gamma\delta=k$ (the product of the roots of a monic quartic is its constant term).
notes: Sign slip: four minus signs give $+$.
$q=-\sum\alpha\beta\gamma$, not the product of the roots.
path: 1.8 Quadratic equations and theory of equations
facts: For $x^4+a_1x^3+a_2x^2+a_3x+a_4=0$: $\sum\alpha=-a_1$, $\sum\alpha\beta=a_2$, $\sum\alpha\beta\gamma=-a_3$, $\alpha\beta\gamma\delta=a_4$.

en.q: If $A$ and $B$ are $3\times3$ real matrices each of rank 2, then the possible values of $\operatorname{rank}(AB)$ are
en.explanation: Sylvester's inequality: $\operatorname{rank}A+\operatorname{rank}B-3\le\operatorname{rank}(AB)\le\min(\operatorname{rank}A,\operatorname{rank}B)$, so $1\le\operatorname{rank}(AB)\le2$. Both occur: $A=B=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,0)$ gives rank 2; $A=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,0)$, $B=\operatorname{diag}(0,1,1)$ gives $AB=\operatorname{diag}(0,1,0)$, of rank 1.
notes: The product can lose rank: $\operatorname{diag}(1,1,0)\operatorname{diag}(0,1,1)$ has rank 1.
path: 2.4 Rank and systems of linear equations
facts: Sylvester: $\operatorname{rank}A+\operatorname{rank}B-n\le\operatorname{rank}(AB)\le\min(\operatorname{rank}A,\operatorname{rank}B)$ for $n\times n$ matrices.

en.q: Given Statement A: $T:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}^2$ defined by $T(a,b,c)=(|a|,0)$ is linear. Statement B: $T:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}^3$ defined by $T(a,b,c)=(a+1,\ b+c,\ 0)$ is linear. Which one of the following is correct?
options: A is true and B is false
A and B both are false
B is true and A is false
A and B both are true
en.explanation: A: $T(-(1,0,0))=(1,0)\ne-T(1,0,0)=(-1,0)$, so not linear. B: $T(0,0,0)=(1,0,0)\ne\vec0$, so not linear. Both statements are false.
facts: A linear map sends $\vec0$ to $\vec0$ and respects scalar multiples; $|a|$ and '$+1$' break this.

en.q: The coefficient of $x^n$ in the expansion of $\log_e(1+3x+2x^2)$ is
en.explanation: $1+3x+2x^2=(1+x)(1+2x)$, so the log is $\log(1+x)+\log(1+2x)$. The coefficient of $x^n$ is $\frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{n}+\frac{(-1)^{n-1}2^n}{n}=\frac{(-1)^{n-1}(2^n+1)}{n}$.
notes: Uses the exponential series instead of the log series.
facts: $\log(1+x)=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{(-1)^{n-1}x^n}{n}$; factorise before expanding.

en.q: $\int_0^1\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2x-1}{1+x-x^2}\right)dx$ is equal to
en.explanation: $\frac{2x-1}{1+x-x^2}=\frac{x-(1-x)}{1+x(1-x)}$, so the integrand is $\tan^{-1}x-\tan^{-1}(1-x)$. By $\int_0^1f(x)dx=\int_0^1f(1-x)dx$, the two parts have equal integrals, so the value is 0.
facts: Spot $\frac{A-B}{1+AB}$ inside $\tan^{-1}$ and split it as $\tan^{-1}A-\tan^{-1}B$.

en.q: The area of the greatest rectangle that can be inscribed in the ellipse $\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ is
en.explanation: Take the vertex $(a\cos\theta,b\sin\theta)$; the rectangle has area $4ab\sin\theta\cos\theta=2ab\sin2\theta$, greatest at $\theta=\frac\pi4$: $2ab$.
notes: Uses the area $2xy$ instead of $4xy$ for the rectangle with vertex $(x,y)$.
facts: Use the parametric point of the ellipse for extreme-value problems.

en.q: The minimum value of $(\sec^{-1}x)^2+(\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x)^2$ is equal to
en.explanation: Let $t=\sec^{-1}x$; then $\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x=\frac\pi2-t$. The sum $t^2+\left(\frac\pi2-t\right)^2=2\left(t-\frac\pi4\right)^2+\frac{\pi^2}8$ is least at $t=\frac\pi4$ ($x=\sqrt2$), giving $\frac{\pi^2}8$.
notes: Value at an end, not the minimum.
facts: $\sec^{-1}x+\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}x=\frac\pi2$ for $|x|\ge1$.

en.q: If $|z+4|\le3$, then the greatest value of $|z+1|$ is
en.explanation: $|z+1|=|(z+4)-3|\le|z+4|+3\le6$, with equality at $z=-7$. So the greatest value is 6.
facts: Triangle inequality: $|z_1-z_2|\le|z_1|+|z_2|$; or: distance from $-1$ to the far end of the disc.

en.q: If $A$ is a $3\times3$ matrix with $|A|=2$, then $|\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A)|$ is
en.explanation: $|\operatorname{adj}B|=|B|^{n-1}$. With $n=3$: $|\operatorname{adj}A|=2^2=4$, then $|\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A)|=4^2=16$.
facts: $|\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A)|=|A|^{(n-1)^2}$.

en.q: $\int\frac{dx}{1+3\sin^2x}$ is equal to ($C$ is an arbitrary constant)
en.explanation: Divide numerator and denominator by $\cos^2x$: $\int\frac{\sec^2x\,dx}{\sec^2x+3\tan^2x}=\int\frac{\sec^2x\,dx}{1+4\tan^2x}$. With $t=\tan x$: $\int\frac{dt}{1+4t^2}=\frac12\tan^{-1}(2t)+C$.
facts: For $\frac1{a+b\sin^2x}$ or $\frac1{a+b\cos^2x}$, divide by $\cos^2x$ and put $t=\tan x$.

en.q: The sum of the first $n$ terms of the series $1^2+2\cdot2^2+3^2+2\cdot4^2+5^2+2\cdot6^2+\cdots$ is $\frac{n(n+1)^2}2$ when $n$ is even. When $n$ is odd, the sum is
en.explanation: If $n$ is odd, $n-1$ is even, so the first $n-1$ terms add to $\frac{(n-1)n^2}2$, and the $n$th term is $n^2$ (odd places carry no factor 2). The sum is $\frac{(n-1)n^2}2+n^2=\frac{n^2(n+1)}2$. Check $n=3$: $1+8+9=18=\frac{9\cdot4}2$.
notes: That is the formula for even $n$.
That is $1^2+2^2+\cdots+n^2$, without the doubled terms.
path: 1.6 Sequences and series: AP, GP, HP
facts: When a series repeats a pattern in pairs, reduce the odd case to the even one: $S_n=S_{n-1}+T_n$.

en.q: The number of symmetric relations on a set with five elements is
en.explanation: A symmetric relation is fixed by choosing which diagonal pairs $(a,a)$ (5 choices, each in or out) and which unordered pairs $\{a,b\}$, $a\ne b$ ($\binom52=10$) to include. So the number is $2^{5+10}=2^{15}$.
notes: That is the number of all relations, $2^{n^2}$.
Counts only subsets of the diagonal.
Counts only the 10 unordered pairs and forgets the diagonal.
facts: On an $n$-set: all relations $2^{n^2}$, reflexive $2^{n^2-n}$, symmetric $2^{n(n+1)/2}$.

en.q: The area of the region bounded by the parabolas $x=-2y^2$ and $x=1-3y^2$ is
en.explanation: They meet where $-2y^2=1-3y^2$, i.e. $y=\pm1$. For $|y|<1$ the curve $x=1-3y^2$ lies to the right. Area $=\int_{-1}^{1}\left[(1-3y^2)-(-2y^2)\right]dy=\int_{-1}^1(1-y^2)\,dy=2-\frac23=\frac43$.
facts: For curves $x=f(y)$, integrate (right − left) with respect to $y$.

en.q: If a $2\times2$ real matrix $A$ has trace 5 and determinant 6, then the trace of $A^2$ is
en.explanation: The eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\lambda_2$ satisfy $\lambda_1+\lambda_2=5$, $\lambda_1\lambda_2=6$ (they are 2 and 3). The eigenvalues of $A^2$ are $\lambda_i^2$, so $\operatorname{tr}A^2=25-2\cdot6=13$.
facts: $\operatorname{tr}A=\sum\lambda_i$, $\det A=\prod\lambda_i$, and $A^k$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_i^k$.

en.q: If $\alpha$ is a root of the equation $x^3+2x^2+gx+1=0$, then $\frac1\alpha$ will also be a root of this equation, when the value of $g$ is
en.explanation: Replacing $x$ by $\frac1x$ gives $x^3+gx^2+2x+1=0$. The roots are closed under $x\mapsto\frac1x$ when this is the same equation, i.e. $g=2$. Then $x^3+2x^2+2x+1=(x+1)(x^2+x+1)$ with roots $-1,\omega,\omega^2$, and indeed $\frac1\omega=\omega^2$.
notes: Correct: the coefficients 1, 2, 2, 1 read the same both ways.
path: 1.8 Quadratic equations and theory of equations
facts: A reciprocal equation has coefficients that are equal from the two ends (or equal and opposite).

en.q: Tangents are drawn from the point $(2,3)$ to the hyperbola $x^2-4y^2=4$. The points of contact are
en.explanation: The chord of contact of $(2,3)$ is $2x-4(3)y=4$, i.e. $x=2+6y$. Substituting: $(2+6y)^2-4y^2=4$ gives $32y^2+24y=0$, so $y=0$ or $y=-\frac34$. The points are $(2,0)$ (tangent $x=2$, vertical) and $\left(-\frac52,-\frac34\right)$ (tangent $5x-6y+8=0$).
notes: On the hyperbola, but its tangent does not pass through $(2,3)$.
The slope form $y=mx\pm\sqrt{a^2m^2-b^2}$ misses the vertical tangent $x=2$.
facts: Use the chord of contact $T=0$; the slope method cannot find a vertical tangent.

en.q: The matrix $\begin{bmatrix}0&3&5-2i\\-3&0&-9\\-5-2i&9&0\end{bmatrix}$ is a
en.explanation: Call the matrix $A$. Its conjugate transpose is $\overline{A}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}0&-3&-5+2i\\3&0&9\\5+2i&-9&0\end{bmatrix}=-A$, so $A$ is skew-Hermitian. It is not skew-symmetric: $a_{13}=5-2i$ but $-a_{31}=5+2i$.
notes: $5-2i$ and $-5-2i$ are not negatives of each other; conjugation is needed.
facts: Hermitian: $\overline{A}^{T}=A$ (real diagonal); skew-Hermitian: $\overline{A}^{T}=-A$ (diagonal entries zero or purely imaginary).

en.q: A smooth sphere of weight $W$ and radius $r$ rests against a smooth vertical wall, supported by a light string of length $l$ joining a point of its surface to a point of the wall. The tension in the string is
en.explanation: The weight (through the centre $O$) and the wall's reaction (normal to the wall, through $O$) meet at $O$, so the string also points at $O$: from its point $A$ on the wall, $AO=l+r$. If $\theta$ is the angle between the string and the wall, $\sin\theta=\frac r{l+r}$ and $\cos\theta=\frac{\sqrt{l^2+2lr}}{l+r}$. Resolving vertically, $T\cos\theta=W$, so $T=\frac{W(l+r)}{\sqrt{l^2+2lr}}$.
notes: That is the reaction of the wall, $W\tan\theta$.
That is $W\cos\theta$; the tension must exceed $W$.
path: 15.2 Three forces in equilibrium: Lami's theorem
facts: Three forces in equilibrium are concurrent (or parallel): a string holding a smooth sphere points through its centre.

en.q: The differential equation of the family of curves $y=\sin(x+c)$, where $c$ is an arbitrary constant, is
en.explanation: One arbitrary constant, so differentiate once: $\frac{dy}{dx}=\cos(x+c)$. Eliminate $c$ with $\sin^2(x+c)+\cos^2(x+c)=1$: $\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2+y^2=1$.
notes: Sign slip: the identity gives a sum, $y^2+\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2=1$.
facts: To form the differential equation of a family with $n$ arbitrary constants, differentiate $n$ times and eliminate them.

en.q: If the coefficients of the $(2r+1)$th and $(r+2)$th terms in the expansion of $(1+x)^{43}$ are equal (the terms being different), then $r$ is
en.explanation: The coefficients are $\binom{43}{2r}$ and $\binom{43}{r+1}$. For different terms, $\binom nk=\binom nl$ with $k\ne l$ needs $k+l=n$: $2r+r+1=43$, so $r=14$. ($r=1$ makes the two terms the same.)
facts: $\binom nk=\binom nl\iff k=l$ or $k+l=n$.

en.q: If $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ are the position vectors of the points $A,B,C$ and $2\vec a+3\vec b-5\vec c=\vec0$, then
options: $A,B,C$ are the vertices of a triangle
en.explanation: $\vec c=\frac{2\vec a+3\vec b}{5}=\frac{3\vec b+2\vec a}{3+2}$, which by the section formula is the point dividing $AB$ internally with $AC:CB=3:2$.
facts: Section formula: $\frac{m\vec b+n\vec a}{m+n}$ divides $AB$ in $m:n$.

en.q: If the curves $ax^2+by^2=1$ and $a'x^2+b'y^2=1$ intersect orthogonally, then
en.explanation: At a common point, slopes are $-\frac{ax}{by}$ and $-\frac{a'x}{b'y}$; orthogonality gives $aa'x^2=-bb'y^2$. Subtracting the equations gives $(a-a')x^2=-(b-b')y^2$. Dividing, $\frac{a-a'}{aa'}=\frac{b-b'}{bb'}$, i.e. $\frac1{a'}-\frac1a=\frac1{b'}-\frac1b$, which rearranges to $\frac1a-\frac1b=\frac1{a'}-\frac1{b'}$.
facts: Curves cut orthogonally when $m_1m_2=-1$ at every common point.

en.q: If $\sigma=(1\ 2\ 3\ 4\ 5\ 6)\in S_6$, then $\sigma^3$ is
en.explanation: $\sigma$ sends each symbol to the next one in the cycle, so $\sigma^3$ moves it three places on: $1\to4\to1$, $2\to5\to2$, $3\to6\to3$. Hence $\sigma^3=(1\ 4)(2\ 5)(3\ 6)$.
notes: Strings the images into one 6-cycle; $\sigma^3$ has order 2, not 6.
path: 4.4 Permutations and the symmetric group Sn
facts: The $k$th power of an $n$-cycle is a product of $\gcd(n,k)$ disjoint cycles, each of length $\frac n{\gcd(n,k)}$.

en.q: If $A=\{(x,y): x^2+y^2=25\}$ and $B=\{(x,y): x^2+9y^2=144\}$, then $A\cap B$ contains
en.explanation: Subtract: $8y^2=119$, so $y^2=\frac{119}8$ and $x^2=25-\frac{119}8=\frac{81}8>0$. Each of $x,y$ has two signs, so $A\cap B$ has 4 points.
notes: The circle is not inside the ellipse: $(5,0)$ lies inside it but $(0,5)$ lies outside.
facts: Points of $A\cap B$ for two curves = common solutions; count the sign choices.

en.q: The lines joining the origin to the points of intersection of the curve $3x^2+5xy-3y^2+2x+3y=0$ and the line $3x-2y=1$ are
en.explanation: Homogenise with $1=3x-2y$: $3x^2+5xy-3y^2+(2x+3y)(3x-2y)=0$, i.e. $9x^2+10xy-9y^2=0$. Since $a+b=9-9=0$, the two lines are perpendicular.
facts: $ax^2+2hxy+by^2=0$ is a pair of perpendicular lines iff $a+b=0$.

en.q: If $T:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}^2$ is any linear transformation, then which of the following is always true?
en.explanation: By rank–nullity, $\operatorname{rank}T+\operatorname{nullity}T=3$ and $\operatorname{rank}T\le2$, so $\operatorname{nullity}T\ge1$: the kernel is non-zero and $T$ is never one-one. The zero map shows the other statements can fail.
facts: Rank–nullity: $\operatorname{rank}T+\operatorname{nullity}T=\dim(\text{domain})$.

en.q: The area of the triangle formed by the lines $x-y=0$ and $x+y=0$ and any tangent to the hyperbola $x^2-y^2=a^2$ is
en.explanation: The tangent at $(a\sec t,a\tan t)$ is $x\sec t-y\tan t=a$. It meets $y=x$ at $x_1=\frac{a}{\sec t-\tan t}$ and $y=-x$ at $x_2=\frac{a}{\sec t+\tan t}$. The triangle with vertices $O$, $(x_1,x_1)$, $(x_2,-x_2)$ has area $\frac12|{-x_1x_2}-x_1x_2|=x_1x_2=\frac{a^2}{\sec^2t-\tan^2t}=a^2$. (Check with the tangent $x=a$: vertices $O,(a,a),(a,-a)$, area $a^2$.)
facts: A tangent to a hyperbola cuts off a triangle of constant area $ab$ with the asymptotes.

en.q: Which of the following linear operators on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is not invertible?
options: The rotation of the plane through $90^\circ$ about the origin
en.explanation: An operator on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is invertible iff its kernel is $\{\vec0\}$ (iff its matrix has non-zero determinant). In the last one $T(1,1)=(0,0)$, so the kernel is the line $y=x$ and $T$ is singular (matrix $\begin{bmatrix}1&-1\\-2&2\end{bmatrix}$, determinant 0). The rotation is undone by the rotation through $-90^\circ$, the reflection is its own inverse, and $\begin{vmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{vmatrix}=-2\ne0$.
notes: Invertible: it is its own inverse.
facts: For $T:V\to V$ with $V$ finite-dimensional: $T$ invertible $\iff\ker T=\{\vec0\}\iff\det[T]\ne0$.

en.q: The angle between the lines $x=1,\ y=2$ and $y=-1,\ z=0$ is
en.explanation: On the line $x=1$, $y=2$ only $z$ varies, so it is parallel to the $z$-axis: direction $(0,0,1)$. On $y=-1$, $z=0$ only $x$ varies: direction $(1,0,0)$. Since $(0,0,1)\cdot(1,0,0)=0$, the angle is $90^\circ$.
notes: Not $30^\circ$: the directions $(0,0,1)$ and $(1,0,0)$ have dot product 0, so $\cos\theta=0$.
Not $60^\circ$ either: $\cos\theta=0$, not $\frac12$; the lines are parallel to the $z$- and $x$-axes.
Correct: the directions are $\hat k$ and $\hat i$.
Not parallel: one line is parallel to the $z$-axis, the other to the $x$-axis.
path: 13.1 Direction cosines and the straight line
facts: The line $x=a$, $y=b$ is parallel to the $z$-axis; write a line in symmetric form to read its direction ratios.

en.q: Forces of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 N act at the centre $O$ of a regular hexagon $A_1A_2A_3A_4A_5A_6$, the force of $k$ N along $OA_k$ ($k=1,2,\dots,6$). The magnitude of their resultant is
en.explanation: Opposite forces combine first: $4-1$, $5-2$, $6-3$ leave three forces of 3 N along $OA_4$, $OA_5$, $OA_6$, at $60^\circ$ to each other. The outer two ($120^\circ$ apart) have resultant 3 N along $OA_5$; adding the middle one gives $3+3=6$ N, along $OA_5$.
notes: Adds the magnitudes as if all acted in one direction.
Combines only two of the three reduced 3 N forces ($60^\circ$ apart).
facts: Cancel opposite forces first; two equal forces $F$ at $120^\circ$ have resultant $F$ along their bisector.

en.q: $\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{x^3+|x|+1}{x^2+2|x|+1}dx$ is equal to
en.explanation: The denominator is $(|x|+1)^2$, an even function. The part $\frac{x^3}{(|x|+1)^2}$ is odd and integrates to 0. The rest is $\frac{|x|+1}{(|x|+1)^2}=\frac1{|x|+1}$, even, giving $2\int_0^1\frac{dx}{1+x}=2\log2$.
notes: Treats the whole integrand as odd.
facts: Split an integrand into odd and even parts over $[-a,a]$.

en.q: If a man can throw a stone up to 196 metre, what will be the time of flight and the maximum height of the stone? ($g=9.8$ metre/sec$^2$)
en.explanation: The greatest range $\frac{u^2}{g}=196$ (at $45^\circ$), so $u^2=196\times9.8$. Time of flight $T=\frac{2u\sin45^\circ}{g}=\sqrt{\frac{2u^2}{g^2}}=\sqrt{\frac{2\times196}{9.8}}=\sqrt{40}=2\sqrt{10}$ s. Height $H=\frac{u^2\sin^245^\circ}{2g}=\frac{196}{4}=49$ m.

en.q: If $x=\sec\theta-\cos\theta$ and $y=\sec^n\theta-\cos^n\theta$, then the value of $(x^2+4)\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2$ is
en.explanation: $\frac{dx}{d\theta}=\tan\theta(\sec\theta+\cos\theta)$ and $\frac{dy}{d\theta}=n\tan\theta(\sec^n\theta+\cos^n\theta)$, so $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{n(\sec^n\theta+\cos^n\theta)}{\sec\theta+\cos\theta}$. notes: No step produces $x^2$: the factor in front of $y^2+4$ is $n^2$, from differentiating $\sec^n\theta$ and $\cos^n\theta$.
facts: $(u+v)^2=(u-v)^2+4uv$: with $uv=1$, $(\sec\theta+\cos\theta)^2=(\sec\theta-\cos\theta)^2+4$.

en.q: The number of $2\times2$ real matrices $A$ such that $A^2=-I$ is
en.explanation: Take $A=\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&-a\end{bmatrix}$; then $A^2=(a^2+bc)I$. Choosing $bc=-1-a^2$, e.g. $A=\begin{bmatrix}a&-(1+a^2)\\1&-a\end{bmatrix}$, gives $A^2=-I$ for every real $a$. So there are infinitely many such matrices (e.g. $\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}$).
notes: Wrong: $A$ cannot be a real scalar matrix, but non-scalar real solutions exist.
facts: $x^2=-1$ has no real number solution, but $A^2=-I$ has infinitely many real $2\times2$ solutions (rotations by $90^\circ$ in any basis).
